opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to where robots can actually matter in people's daily lives, and where the hardest, most interesting problems are.

For a long time, robotics lived in factories. Those environments are structured on purpose: the parts arrive in the same place, the lighting is controlled, and the task repeats millions of times. That's great for industrial automation, but it means the robot doesn't really need to understand the world. The world has been engineered around the robot.

The home is the opposite. Every home is different, and the same home is different from one day to the next. There are clothes on the floor, dishes in odd places, pets and kids moving around, and objects that are soft, deformable, or fragile. If you want a robot that is truly general, that can perceive, reason, and manipulate in an open-ended world, the home is a kind of ultimate test. If you can work reliably there, you've solved a lot of the core problems in robotics along the way.

There's also the human side. So much of our time goes into household labor: cooking, cleaning, laundry, tidying up, caring for elderly family members. Much of it is repetitive and physically tiring, and it isn't evenly shared. Aging populations make the need even sharper. A robot that can really help at home could give people back hours of their lives every week, and help older people live independently for longer. In terms of impact, it's hard to think of a more direct way robotics could touch everyone.

And the timing feels right. Over the past few years, learning-based methods, large models, and better and cheaper hardware have changed what's possible. We're moving from hand-programming each behavior toward robots that learn from data and demonstrations and can generalize. That makes the home, which used to seem impossibly messy, feel like a realistic target rather than science fiction.

So for me it's natural on both counts. Scientifically, it's the frontier that forces us to build robots that really understand and adapt. Practically, it's where they could improve the most people's lives. That combination is what draws me to it.

r001.rationale: The response describes the home as an ultimate test that exposes core robotics challenges, but it does not propose using household problems current robots cannot solve to identify research directions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the home is where the hardest and most interesting problems in robotics actually live, and that's exactly why it's a natural destination rather than a distant dream.

For a long time, robotics made progress by controlling the environment. In a factory, you fix the lighting, you fix the position of every part, you fence off the humans, and the robot repeats one motion a million times. That works, but it's a bit of a trick. The robot isn't really perceiving or deciding anything. The intelligence is in the engineering of the setup around it.

The home is the opposite. Every kitchen is laid out differently. Objects are soft, transparent, cluttered, half-hidden behind other objects. A cup is sometimes on the counter and sometimes in the sink with water in it. There are children and pets moving around unpredictably. Nothing is fixed. So if you want to make a robot that works in a home, you can't rely on the environment doing the work for you. The robot itself has to generalize, has to perceive, has to recover from mistakes. In other words, the home forces you to solve the actual problem of robotics instead of engineering around it.

There's also a demand-side reason. If you ask what people would genuinely want a physical machine to do for them, the answers are overwhelmingly domestic: cook, clean, fold laundry, take care of an aging parent. Those are tasks that consume hours of every person's life, every day, in every country. The population is aging, labor costs are rising, and there's no software-only solution to loading a dishwasher. So the pull is enormous.

And finally, I think the timing matters. Five or ten years ago, saying "household robot" sounded naive because perception was too brittle. But the progress in large models has changed what's possible. We now have systems that understand language, understand scenes, and can map that understanding onto actions. The missing piece has shifted from "can the robot see" to "can the robot act reliably in a messy physical world." That's a hard problem, but it's a tractable one, and the home is the best place to confront it.

So for me it's not a leap. It's where the field was always going. We just finally have the tools to take it seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says homes expose difficult robotics problems and require robots to generalize, perceive, and recover, but it does not propose using household tasks current robots cannot solve to identify research directions.

astra-6.text:
I think the home is a natural direction because it’s where robots could become useful in our everyday lives. We spend so much time on routine tasks—cleaning, tidying up, moving things around—and help with those tasks could make a real difference, especially for people who have difficulty doing them themselves.

At the same time, a home is a very challenging environment for a robot. Every home is different, objects move, and people do things you can’t predict. So bringing robots into homes pushes us to develop systems that can adapt, work safely around people, and be useful beyond a carefully controlled setting.

r001.rationale: The response describes household tasks and unpredictable homes as challenges that motivate adaptable, safe systems, but it does not propose using problems current robots cannot solve to identify research directions.

sol-6.1.text: I think the home is a natural place for robotics because it’s where so much of everyday life happens. If we want robots to be useful to people, they need to help with ordinary tasks in the environments where people actually live. It’s also a challenging research setting: every home is different, things move around, and people don’t always behave predictably. A robot has to do more than execute a fixed motion—it has to understand the situation, adapt, and interact safely with people. That makes the home both a meaningful application and a rich place to study robotics.

r001.rationale: The response describes the home as a challenging setting for robotics research, but does not propose using household problems that current robots cannot solve to identify research directions.
